items.title: Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits
items.summary: The slowed Starlink connections had affected the Ukraine's military and drone operations for a week.
items.content:
Image caption, Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations
Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.
Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.
This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".
Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.
"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.
Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war .
Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea.
Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.
They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled
Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.
Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).
The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.
Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .
Waves generated by Typhoon Champi crash against a seawall in Keelung. Photograph: Ann Wang/Reuters Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.
Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.
Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.
Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

items.title: White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom
items.summary: From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on some products, including certain machinery, and placed on others, such as carpets.
items.content:
Image caption, Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war
The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.
From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.
Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.
The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (Â£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.
Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".
Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.
The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".
It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".
Image caption, Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections
Trump "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce", White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.
Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."
The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.
Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner".
She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".
Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."
Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.
Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.
Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a â trade âdeal with the US.
Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out.
"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that."
LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

items.title: Turmoil hits AI buildout as neoclouds face pressure, credit risks mount and Solidigm pulls IPO
items.summary: Stock slumps, pulled IPOs and rising spreads on credit default swaps this week sets stage for hyperscaler earnings.
items.content:
AI turmoil: neoclouds struggle, credit risks jump, Solidigm pulls IPO
Concerns over the AI trade dragged the Nasdaq down this week, with neoclouds posting some of the steepest losses.
Debt markets are roiling, with Meta, Oracle and Nvidia facing the largest-ever spreads on credit default swaps linked to their corporate bonds.
SK Hynix abandoned plans for an IPO of its Solidigm unit.
CoreWeave founder and CEO Mike Intrator poses for a photo during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq headquarters in New York, March 28, 2025.
Neoclouds tanked. Credit default swaps soared. Meta turned cash flow negative. And SK Hynix's Solidigm unit canceled plans for its initial public offering.
It's been a rocky week for the AI infrastructure trade.
The Nasdaq followed Thursday's beating with an additional drop on Friday to end the week down 0.7%. Among the hyperscalers, the worst performer was Alphabet , shares of which sank 6% ahead of the internet giant's third-quarter earnings report next week. Microsoft and Amazon are also on the docket, and they each saw shares fall less than 1%.
While the tech market has thus far avoided a dramatic across-the-board sell-off, the artificial intelligence buildout is showing signs of strain.
Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN all fell sharply this week, bringing their losses for October to well over 30% each. CoreWeave, the leader of the pack, has seen spreads on its CDS widen past 11%, generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default.
Meanwhile, yields on the company's 2031 and 2032 unsecured notes topped 15% .
"What investors are doing is throwing every baby out with the bathwater and saying anyone who is a neocloud" will be devalued, Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Thursday.
Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza on the problem with neoclouds
Fears aren't limited to the U.S. market. Shares of Elice Group, a South Korean cloud provider, dropped 30% in their market debut on Tuesday, and shares of Australia's NextDC plunged 39.5% on Wednesday after the data center operator slashed its annual earnings forecast.
AI optimism has been the major market driver for the past couple of years, as unrelenting demand for new models and services pushes the world's biggest tech companies to spend on infrastructure at historic rates. However, skeptics are getting more vocal in their concerns that returns on AI investment won't justify the capital expenditures.
Analysts at research and advisory firm Gartner predict that 80% of neocloud companies will either cease operations or be absorbed by 2030.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , perhaps the leading AI evangelist, remains bullish. Huang said this week at a company conference in Berlin that "demand for the neoclouds is off the charts."
"The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal . "That's going to get solved."
Wall Street isn't convinced. On Thursday, South Korean memory giant SK Hynix , one of the biggest winners in the AI boom, said it's pulling an IPO for its U.S.-based Solidigm unit, citing market volatility. SK Hynix purchased Solidigm, which makes NAND and SSD storage for data centers, from Intel in 2021.
"While an IPO was expected to ease investment burdens and expand capacity for shareholder returns, the review has been discontinued in light of market conditions and share price trends," SK Hynix said in a release .
Despite the turmoil, all of tech's mega-caps have maintained their investment-grade rating even as they've opened their wallets to fuel their build-outs, including through debt. Even with that group of companies, the market is showing some jitters.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.
Meta saw its stock plunge 7% on Thursday after the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter of over $2 billion while raising the floor of its full-year capex to $135 billion from $130 billion. Meta also said it plans to spend about $825 billion over the coming years on various leases and contracts, with over $450 billion of those leases being non-cancellable take-or-pay agreements.
Spreads on Meta's five-year CDS reached all-time highs of over 124 basis points. CDS on Nvidia and Oracle also touched records, with their spreads hitting 126 basis points and 343 basis points, respectively, this week. Oracle's stock has lost over one-third of its value this year, and now the company faces risks of a credit rating downgrade .
John Williams, who leads the derivatives practice at law firm Milbank LLP, says investors are seeking numerous ways beyond buying CDS to hedge their bets with respect to the AI trade.
"There's so much investment going into it that it's just very appropriate to look for risk management tools, completely regardless of whether you're bullish or bearish," Williams said. "It would be crazy for people not to be looking for appropriate risk management tools for it."
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, told CNBC's "SquawkBox Asia" last week that it's "all kind of tied together," referring to AI's impact on the whole market.
"Can you drop a bowling ball in one part of the pool and not get any waves downstream to the rest of the Nasdaq?" he said. "I don't know. I have some concern about that."
— CNBC's Katie Tarasov contributed to this report

China is an important trading partner for North Korea and its leader Kim Jong Un [File: AFP]
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has returned home after a day trip to the Chinese border city of Dandong, state news agency Xinhua has reported, following a symbolic crossing over a newly opened bridge.
Kim was accompanied during his visit on Saturday by China’s fourth-highest-ranked official, Wang Huning, who conveyed “cordial greetings and best wishes” from Chinese President Xi Jinping, according to Xinhua.

The visit came about a week after the New Yalu River Bridge linking the two countries was officially opened, 12 years after its completion, deepening economic ties between the Asian giant and its small, nuclear-armed neighbour.
Kim’s visit also coincided with the eve of the anniversary of China’s entry into the 1950–1953 Korean War.
Kim and Wang visited a Korean War memorial in Dandong, where the North Korean leader paid tribute to Chinese soldiers who fought alongside North Korea during the conflict, Xinhua reported.
The two also toured a local auto factory and pledged to strengthen bilateral relations.
Pyongyang “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand their practical cooperation,” Kim said, according to Xinhua.
Wang later accompanied Kim to the new bridge to bid farewell to the North Korean leader.
Analysts say the trip reflects Kim’s increasingly assertive foreign policy, as he seeks to align Pyongyang with Beijing and Moscow in a united front against the United States, in what he portrays as a “new Cold War”.
Experts said the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu River, was a key symbol of strengthening ties between the two countries and reflected their intent to expand trade. It is expected to accommodate two-way traffic around the clock, including container shipments and heavy cargo trucks.
The four-lane structure was completed in 2014, but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, according to South Korean news reports.
“The opening of the bridge has resolved a major bottleneck in China-North Korea trade logistics,” Lu Chao, an expert in China-North Korea relations at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, a Chinese government think tank in Shenyang, told the Reuters news agency.
“With the logistics constraint eased, bilateral trade is likely to increase further,” Lu said.
China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a vital source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the reclusive state, although ties have not always been smooth.
China, which fought alongside North Korea in the Korean War, is Pyongyang’s main economic and diplomatic backer. However, North Korea has drawn closer to Russia since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which analysts say has reduced Pyongyang’s reliance on Beijing.
Kim’s last known visit to China was in September 2025 to attend the 80th Victory Day celebrations in Beijing, where he held a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Xi made a state visit to North Korea in June in which he expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

French police arrested almost 1,000 people on Saturday during the protests held across the country, interior minister Laurent Nunez said.
He told reporters that the number “will rise” as more data from police becomes available.
Although marches over the cost of living “passed off well” in cities, officers found themselves later confronted with “an extremely elevated level of violence” from “ultra-left” groups, Nunez said.

A peaceful protest during the day in Paris descended into violent clashes with police by the time night fell.
The sound of pop music blaring and chanted slogans was swapped for the sound of teargas being released and fireworks being released, according to reports.
Eyewitnesses say the mood soured at the end of the march, where rows of police officers and vans awaited the crowd.
Protesters reportedly fired fireworks towards law enforcement officers, who responded with charges and baton strikes.
Students involved in a Paris demonstration questioned the police response Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters The AFP news agency quoted David, a protester who gave only his first name. He is said to have appeared shaken and had a gash on his face, which he said was caused by a police officer throwing a baton at him.
“The police started moving towards everyone, telling them to get down and back off. They were just taking people down, you know, beating protesters,” he said.
Mike, a 23-year-old student who also declined to give his surname, said: “Look around, they’re just teenagers. Is it normal for teenagers to be teargassed and beaten with batons?”
For Jessica, a 24-year-old student, said: “I just don’t understand why there’s so much violence. I feel like our right to protest is being trampled on.”
As night fell, police began clearing the streets and protesters started to disperse.
Italian police said nine people were arrested, and 371 briefly detained during protests in eight cities.
In a statement, the police said 110 of those either arrested or detained were minors.
My colleague Angelique Chrisafis has been reporting from the protest in Paris today, which has since dispersed.
She writes about how a largely peaceful demonstration on the outskirts of the French capital was marred at the end by violence.
The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.
But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.
A man reportedly had his fingers blown off during trouble in France , a minister has said.
France’s interior minister – equivalent to the home secretary in the UK – Laurent Nunez said two people had been “seriously injured” during what he called “an extremely elevated level of violence” at today’s protests.
A 20-year-old man in Toulouse, in southern France, is said to have had his fingers blown off, and the other serious injury occurred in Clermont-Ferrand in the centre of the country. He did not give details of either case.
In an update, Nunez said “ultra-left” groups had thrown projectiles and aimed fireworks at police to provoke clashes.
Projectiles were thrown during Saturday’s clashes between protesters and police Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters He struck a more positive tone than last week when violence erupted across French cities during protests about the level of investment into public services and the cost of living.
Nunez said that, while some shops and businesses had been vandalised and looted today, “the scale was far smaller” than a week earlier. He stressed that shopping centres had been well protected this time.
In Paris, where the main demonstration passed off largely peacefully but clashes broke out with police as the crowd dispersed, Nunez said “several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including about 500 individuals identified as rioters”.
Ensuing clashes in the French capital lasted for around two hours, he said.
The minister said that there were first-time clashes in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier between far-right activists who sought confrontations with “ultra-left militants” who he said claimed to be there to protect businesses.
The authorities will remain “on high alert” through the night and into Sunday, he said.
Demonstrations were held in the Italian cities of Rome, Turin and elsewhere, with some turning violent.
As we reported earlier, security was heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.
A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards.
Protesters in Rome attempted to force themselves into the Colosseum Photograph: Vincenzo Livieri/Reuters Elsewhere in the city, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters after unrest last week, particularly in Milan.
Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association, said: “I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study … and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities.”
A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organisers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.
But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organisers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and teargas.
In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about 500m away.
French police arrested almost 1,000 people on Saturday during the protests held across the country, interior minister Laurent Nunez said.
He told reporters that the number “will rise” as more data from police becomes available.
Although marches over the cost of living “passed off well” in cities, officers found themselves later confronted with “an extremely elevated level of violence” from “ultra-left” groups, Nunez said.
France's interior minister Laurent Nunez has given an update on the number of arrests at Saturday’s protests Photograph: Julien de Rosa/EPA Jean-Luc Mélenchon , the radical-left presidential candidate who marched in the Paris rally today, said in a social media post that the French police “ruined the day” by “shooting indiscriminately” at Paris protesters.
“In Paris, as a way to ruin the day and blow off some steam, the so-called ‘forces of law and order’ are firing tear gas and shooting indiscriminately into the crowd at the tail end of the march, all to secure footage for domestic television channels, which have spent the entire week broadcasting the very images that incited the killer in Trappes,” he wrote. “A non-stop display of shame.”
In addition to the earlier footage of police using tear gas against protesters in Lyon, we are now seeing tear gas being deployed in the cities of Paris, Marseille, Nantes, and Bordeaux.
Though the protests have been relatively contained so far, the use of tear gas has become an increasingly common tactic for police to disperse crowds at the end of organized rallies, even without an immediate threat. And taking past demonstrations into consideration, these situations often become more volatile as the sun begins setting and the organized gatherings are ending.
French gendarmes stand in position amid tear gas and clashes during a demonstration organized by labour unions in Paris as part of nationwide protests in France, October 24, 2026. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters View image in fullscreen
A man runs amid tear gas during a demonstration in Lyon, France, October 24, 2026. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters View image in fullscreen
Masked protesters take cover behind a plywood board amid clashes and tear gas during a demonstration organized by labour unions in Paris, France, October 24, 2026. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters The Interior Ministry has put today’s nationwide turnout at 410,000 total protesters across France .
Clashes began to erupt late on Saturday, following a pattern of otherwise peaceful protests growing more tempestuous as the day draws to a close.
The Paris march began calmly, but near its endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people.
Authorities had confined the capital’s march to the city’s southeastern edge, keeping protesters away from central neighborhoods hit by last weekend’s destruction.
Police in Paris say that about 110,000 people have marched across France’s capital today, but that the “situation remains calm” according to reporting from AFP. Authorities have now begun dispersing the crowds.
The 110,000 figure is roughly the same amount as the number of protesters in Paris last weekend. Considering the fears many people had that the protests could turn violent, as well as the rainy weather across the area, the number is an impressive showing.
The police also said more than 3,000 checks have been carried out and 65 people were arrested during the demonstrations in Paris.
Meanwhile in Albania , more than 2000 police have been deployed around Tirana on the 12th day of student-led protests amid reports of concerted efforts to stop demonstrators entering the capital.
Protests initially spurred by fury over a planned Trump family-backed resort in Albania have turned increasingly violent as students have joined what growing numbers are now calling a revolution to oust prime minister Edi Rama. Today, rally numbers swelled with demonstrators traveling to Tirana from cities across the Balkan state and as teachers, doctors and labour unions also weighed in.
But police also stand increasingly accused of heavy-handed tactics amid reports of civilians being plucked from the streets by masked officers and riot police increasingly resorting to using rubber bullets, batons, tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.
Speaking to the Guardian after spending several hours at Tirana’s National Trauma hospital earlier in the day, Kei Brisku, who heads the Abania Rehabilitation Centre for Trauma and Torture, said there were growing concerns about “the mass and random use” of rubber bullets.
“Nine protestors, five women and four men, were badly wounded by rubber bullets today and are now in hospital,” he said.
“The use of rubber bullets against violent protesters may be justified under applicable regulations ... however, their indiscriminate use against crowds is unacceptable, as it risks harming peaceful protesters and bystanders who pose no threat.”
In power for 13 years, Rama has resolutely refused to resign. While he has offered to discuss the “ legitimate concerns” of students, he has ruled out talking with hooligans who resort to violence.
Last week, the socialist leader told the Guardian the “violence in Tirana is very real,” as he dismissed accusations that his government was employing underhand tactics to fast-track the controversial resort championed by Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law.
The NFL (American football league) closed its “NFL House” in Paris as the city braced for street protests with a heavy police presence and storefronts boarded up.
The league announced the closure to fans on Saturday morning through its “OnePass” app, according to the AP, citing “potential accessibility issues.”
Security concerns have overshadowed the NFL’s planned debut in Paris. The New Orleans Saints will play the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in the league’s first-ever regular-season game in France.
Major museums including the Louvre and Orsay Museum are also closed Saturday, though tourists were seen lined up to enter Notre Dame Cathedral.
Former Pittsburgh Steelers player Donte Stallworth participates in the Hail Mary event on the banks of the Seine river in Paris, Friday, 23 October, 2026 in the build up to the Saints against Steelers NFL game. Photograph: Dave Shopland/AP View image in fullscreen
Thousands of pensioners and retirees protesting for pension protections in Madrid Photograph: Aaron Heredia/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Spanish authorities say about 25,000 demonstrators have marched through the country’s capital demanding protections to the state pension scheme.
Spain is voting in a snap parliamentary election in a few weeks and this has been a key topic of concern. Spain’s Socalist prime minister Pedro Sanchez, who called the snap election after struggling to get pension reforms through parliament, has accused conservative parties of holding back inflation-linked increases.
Protesters marched from the Atocha train station to the Gran Via shopping avenue in the Spanish capital.
Some expressed concern about portions of their state pensions being privatised in the future. About 6.8 million Spaniards receive a state pension and fiscally conservative, right-wing politicians have raised questions over how sustainable the current system is.
Spain has also seem major protests in recent months over increasingly unaffordable housing and renters’ rights.
Some are, namely in certain cities and low-income suburbs. Videos filmed by students and teachers have shown leaks, scurrying rats, holes in walls and ceilings, broken toilets and not enough chairs or tables, meaning teachers have to carry them from classroom to classroom. Some children said they had to learn in class while leaks were pouring into buckets, or move desks to avoid getting wet. Many school classrooms experienced temperatures over 35C (95F) in the heatwaves of last May and June.
Estimates in recent years have pointed to thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, in need of repair. These include many 1960s school buildings. French regions are responsible for upkeep of high school buildings, but have asked for higher budgets from the government. A senate report has advised that billions need to be spent in the coming years to renovate and repair schools, as well as to address the impact of the climate crisis.
How dilapidated are French schools and how bad is inequality in the education system?
Tens of thousands of people have turned out to the heavily policed demonstrations across France and they have been, on the whole, quite contained so far.
Some sections of the crowd could be seen singing and dancing in Paris as they walked along the route, which was pushed to the city’s fringes at the last minute as police sought to move the march away from the fortified city centre.
In Lyon , police used teargas early on in the banned demonstration to disperse some of the crowd but people were still able to walk on.
In the last half hour there’s also a been of bit of rough activity in Marseille between police and a few dozen people. The French broadcaster BFMTV has shown live footage of masked attendees throwing bins, flares going off and spot fires in the street. There are cordons of riot police around.
Overall though, the heavy policing has appeared to be successful so far in staving off the type of looting, ransacking and violent activity we saw on the fringes of the marches last week. The government has added on 20% more officers, for a 70,000 strong force across the country.
Earlier today, the French interior minister had said protest numbers – at about 36,000 in the morning- were about half of what they were last Saturday.
At the Paris march, Nadège, a communications worker, said she was at Place de la République last Saturday when teargas hit. But that hadn’t deterred her.
I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now.
We have to keep our rights alive. We’ve seen what happens in the US when a bad president is in power. In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.
Photograph: Angelique Chrisafis/The Guardian The French president had hosted student representatives for a highly anticipated meeting yesterday afternoon.
Going in, the student leaders had already expressed cynicism over whether the French president would adequately address their concerns.
Pupils in Paris began protests over the quality of their education four weeks ago – and their spirit has since inspired demonstrations elsewhere, across the nation and also into other countries, such as Italy and Greece.
French high schoolers say they’re fed up with the deteriorating state of their school buildings, overworked and underpaid teachers, and packed classrooms.
They’re demanding school renovations and upgrades, better study conditions and the scrapping of the Parcoursup univeristy admissions platform which was introduced in 2018 and has long been criticised for lack of transparency.
Macron held a two-and-a-half hours-long meeting with 20 students.
Nathanael Combary, president of campaign group High School Renewal, said the president had been “attentive” and they would continue talks with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday on proposed changes like reform of Parcoursup.
But he and other student leaders called on their peers to continue protesting this weekend.
Student leader Nathanael Combary was one of 20 representatives who met with Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace on Friday for negotiations. Photograph: Jeanne Accorsini/SIPA/Shutterstock The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the La France Insoumise party, is also marching in the Parisian procession.
Speaking to the press earlier he said the protests would continue every week until Emmanuel Macron and his government addressed the public’s demands.
He said Macron “is going to understand that this is going to repeat itself every week” and urged the president, “there is still time for him to concede” to the students’ wishes.
Macron met with student leaders on Friday for the first time since the demonstrations began a month ago. More on that meeting next.

Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris Close
Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday.
A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as protesters were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police.
Around 70,000 officers were deployed across France for a second consecutive weekend and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.
The Interior Ministry estimated around 400,000 people took part in Saturday's demonstrations, with nearly 1,000 arrests made.
Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon.

Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?
Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink? Close
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky says unexplained limits on Starlink and Starshield services continue to affect Ukrainian forces, while US officials and Elon Musk offer conflicting accounts of who controls the restrictions.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.
The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
The BBC's Washington correspondent Daniel Bush looks at what officials have said about the technology.

The US and Israel's war on Iran, ongoing since February, has never been particularly popular. But two new polls show that as voters prepare for the November 3 midterm elections, they're thinking about it—and Americans say it's priority for it to be over.
An AP-NORC poll released earlier this week shows about seven in ten voters believe the government should prioritize ending the war. Their other primary concern is costs: eight in ten say lowering the cost of living should be one of the highest priorities for the next session of Congress coming up. Those concerns are intertwined: surging fuel prices, airfares, and mortgage rates have cost each American household an average of $2,000 , Moody's estimated this week. The AP-NORC result follows a Fox News poll released in September that found six in ten Americans oppose military action against Iran.
Trump doesn't seem to care. At a recent campaign rally in Greenville, North Carolina, the president claimed that "our gas prices are lower than under Obama, and they're lower than Sleepy Joe Biden." The average price of a gallon of gas was $2.95 during Obama's second term. It was $3.47 under Biden. Right now, that same gallon costs about $4.30 .
"Iran's killed many, many Americans, many, many people throughout the world for a long time, they were the bully of the Middle East. They were one of the bullies of the world. They're not a bully anymore," Trump went on to say. The death toll in Iran has reached at least 3,400, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs; 33,000 people have been injured.
Iran, Trump asserted, is "the worst country in the world—and our gas prices, it's a small thing to pay." More than 70 percent of Americans, the Fox News poll found, don't think Trump has a plan to end the war. But Trump's already fantasizing about his next war: this time, he wants to attack Cuba.
"Don't worry, we'll take care of Cuba on our way back from Iran," Trump said at an October 23 rally in Fort Myers, Florida. The ongoing US embargo on Cuba—which intensified in January of 2026—has caused the electrical grid to collapse, made basic medications inaccessible, and imposed starvation on the Cuban people. That embargo has been described as an act of siege warfare , but Trump's threats yesterday to bring warships to Cuba constitute a new level of aggression.
We'll do a little stopover," he said. "We're going to come back from Iran, those beautiful ships. We'll pass Cuba. We'll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They'll raise up their hands, and then we're going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the job."

items.content:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
Hezbollah is leveraging several political and informational lines of effort to deter the Lebanese government from prosecuting the group for a recent smuggling operation, which Hezbollah likely fears could establish a precedent for legal action against its illicit activities.
Hezbollah’s lines of effort are indicative of the challenges that face the government as it attempts to confront Hezbollah but do not guarantee that Hezbollah will succeed in breaking the government's will to disarm and prosecute the group in this instance.
Iraq-based Axis of Resistance actors have very likely launched at least four drones targeting Saudi Arabia within the past 20 days. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and other regional countries from Iraq by any Iranian partner or proxy support Iranian objectives to compel the United States to end the war in terms favorable to Iran by imposing increasing costs on US partners and allies in the region.
Saudi Arabia is expanding the scope of its air campaign in Yemen by interdicting Houthi smuggling cargo that could sustain Houthi military activities against the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia.
Hezbollah is leveraging several political and informational lines of effort to deter the Lebanese government from prosecuting the group for a recent smuggling operation, which Hezbollah likely fears could establish a precedent for legal action against its illicit activities. The Lebanese government is investigating the group after Lebanese Internal Security Forces (ISF) personnel interdicted a Hezbollah truck carrying nearly 800 kilograms of high explosives from the Bekaa Valley to Beirut's southern suburbs on October 5.[1] The government currently seeks to refer the criminal case to the Judicial Council, which is Lebanon's highest criminal court, and prosecute the Hezbollah members involved in smuggling explosives.[2] Referring the case to the Judicial Council would break Hezbollah’s de facto legal immunity and expose the organization to potential legal consequences.[3] Hezbollah accordingly likely views the possible legal actions that the government is exploring as steps that could progress or even hasten existing government efforts to disarm the group entirely under the June 2026 Agreement, particularly by establishing a precedent for legal action against Hezbollah’s illicit activities.[4] Lebanese government success in holding Hezbollah accountable for smuggling weapons threatens Hezbollah’s ability to resupply itself with impunity and maintain its arms.[5] The successful prosecution of the case could also strengthen the government’s confidence and preparedness to further challenge Hezbollah’s military and criminal activities, potentially to the point of military disarmament.
Hezbollah is attempting to exploit the Lebanese government’s sensitivity toward civil conflict by threatening the government with unrest and portraying the government as sectarian and beholden to Israeli interests. Hezbollah’s parliamentary bloc warned on October 23 that Lebanon is liable to “fragmentation” and suggested that the government is pushing Lebanon toward civil conflict in pursuing legal action against Hezbollah.[6] Hezbollah officials further derided the government’s efforts as “settling internal sectarian scores.”[7] The Hezbollah officials also called any attempt to arrest Hezbollah officials an “act of Israeli aggression,” which is likely also a veiled threat to confront government police or military action.[8] Hezbollah has historically used these kinds of threats and rhetoric to render the Lebanese government and public unwilling to threaten the group’s military organization.[9] The government is particularly sensitive to such threats given Lebanon’s history of civil war and sectarian violence.[10]
Hezbollah also leveraged its political alliance with Parliament Speaker and Hezbollah ally Nabih Berri, who leads the Shia Amal Movement, to delay President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam’s efforts to prosecute Hezbollah on October 22.[11] Lebanese media reported on October 23 that Berri urged Aoun and Salam to postpone a necessary cabinet vote that would refer the Hezbollah explosives case to the Judicial Council, which answers to the pro-government Justice Minister and issues binding rulings without appeal.[12] Berri reportedly promised Aoun and Salam that, in return for postponing the cabinet vote, Hezbollah would neither foment civil conflict nor trigger a government crisis by withdrawing Hezbollah and Amal from the cabinet.[13] The Lebanese ISF and Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) will continue to investigate the incident during this postponement under the Lebanese Military Court’s jurisdiction.[14] The Military Court is led by Brigadier General Wassim Fayad, who is reportedly close to Hezbollah and has previously obstructed prosecutions under pressure from the group.[15]
Hezbollah’s lines of effort illustrate the challenges facing the Lebanese government as it attempts to confront the group, but these efforts do not guarantee that Hezbollah will succeed in breaking the government's will to disarm and prosecute the group in this instance. Hezbollah is relying on lines of effort that have succeeded during previous efforts to hold the group accountable over the last two decades.[16] Hezbollah is far weaker and less popular now than it was during some of these previous efforts, however, because it has exhausted much of its military strength and popular support since October 2023 by initiating destructive wars with Israel.[17] The Lebanese government is also demonstrating resolve to counter Hezbollah’s threats and thwart its illicit activities, including by authorizing ISF raids and LAF deployments in Beirut’s southern suburbs, which are a historical Hezbollah stronghold.[18] ISW-CTP has outlined Hezbollah’s lines of effort to avoid disarmament and vulnerabilities that the United States and Lebanon can exploit in an October 22 special report (read the full report here: How Hezbollah is Preventing its Disarmament, Again .)[19]
Saudi Arabia is expanding the scope of its air campaign in Yemen by interdicting Houthi smuggling cargo that could sustain Houthi military operations against the internationally recognized Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia.[20] Saudi coalition aircraft reportedly struck a likely Houthi smuggling vessel near Houthi-controlled Zuqar Island in the Red Sea on October 22.[21] Saudi coalition aircraft have increasingly targeted Houthi smuggling vessels in the Red Sea since October 16.[22] The Saudi Joint Forces Command also issued a statement warning Yemeni vessels against supporting Houthi smuggling efforts on October 19.[23] The Houthis have established an extensive international smuggling network, with support from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC), to acquire small arms, drone and missile components, and other military equipment in recent years.[24] Saudi interdiction efforts likely aim to prevent arms and equipment that the Houthis could use to resupply frontline units from reaching the group by interdicting vessels carrying illicit cargo. The Houthis could also theoretically use drone and missile equipment acquired through smuggling to supply Houthi missile and drone units that are conducting daily attacks on Saudi critical infrastructure (see below).
The increase in Saudi airstrikes targeting Houthi smuggling assets comes amid challenges to the Yemeni government’s ability to conduct maritime counter-smuggling operations. The Yemeni-government-aligned, Saudi-backed National Resistance Forces historically relied upon its positions on the Red Sea coast, and at Mokha port in particular, as a base for the Yemeni government's maritime counter-smuggling operations in the Red Sea. The Houthis seized this coastline, including Mokha, on September 10.[25] The loss of Yemeni-controlled territory and port infrastructure along the Red Sea coast has almost certainly limited the Yemeni government's ability to conduct anti-smuggling operations against the Houthis.[26] It is also unclear if government forces have had the bandwidth to conduct such counter-smuggling operations while forces are currently engaged in a full mobilization against the Houthis.

Iraq-based Axis of Resistance actors have very likely launched at least four drones targeting Saudi Arabia within the past 20 days.[27] Saudi security sources told US-funded regional media on October 22 that the drones targeted unspecified “vital sites.”[28] Saudi Arabia has reportedly informed the Iraqi federal government of the attacks.[29] The report did not specify where in Iraq the launches originated, but Iraqi authorities have reportedly increased surveillance over militia sites in Maysan Province over the past two weeks that they suspect Iranian-backed Iraqi militias are using to conduct attacks.[30] IRGC-managed Iraqi militia cells based along the Iraq-Iran border, including in Maysan Province, have conducted multiple attacks on neighboring countries in recent months, including a September 10 attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline.[31] The Houthis, who maintain an active presence in Iraq, reportedly coordinated some of these cross-border attacks with Iraqi militias.[32] It is possible that Iraqi fighters, Houthi fighters, or a combination of Iraqi and Houthi forces launched the drones at Saudi Arabia. Attacks on Saudi Arabia and other regional countries from Iraq by any Iranian partner or proxy support Iranian objectives to compel the United States to end the war in terms favorable to Iran by imposing increasing costs on US partners and allies in the region, including by imposing economic costs through attacks on energy infrastructure.
Yemeni government-aligned forces continued to advance into contested territory south of Taiz City, likely to try to break the Houthis’ encirclement of government-aligned forces in central Taiz Governorate. Yemeni government-aligned forces advanced to Jabal Manara in al Misrakh District on October 22, which the Houthis previously occupied, according to Yemeni and DC-based Yemen analyst sources.[33] Yemeni government-aligned forces have advanced into al Misrakh District and engaged Houthi fighters in the area in recent days, likely in order to try to break the Houthis' encirclement of central Taiz Governorate. The Houthis fully encircled the city on October 12.[34]
Yemeni government-aligned forces’ advances into al Misrakh District come amid the continued success of Yemeni government-aligned forces’ efforts to repel Houthi advances into the “Old Airport” neighborhood on the western outskirts of Taiz City on October 22.[35] Yemeni government-aligned forces similarly repelled Houthi attempts to advance into the area on October 17 and 18.[36] The “Old Airport” neighborhood sits along a major road leading into Taiz City that the Houthis have sought to capture in recent weeks.[37]
The Houthis have continued to attack targets across Saudi Arabia to impose economic and political costs on Saudi Arabia and compel Saudi Arabia to capitulate to Houthi demands. The Saudi Joint Forces Command reported that Saudi air defenses intercepted one ballistic missile over Najran, southern Saudi Arabia, on October 22.[38] Saudi air defenses also intercepted two ballistic missiles over Riyadh and Khamis Mushait and two drones over Saudi Arabia’s southern region on October 23.[39] The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil facilities, airports, and other civilian infrastructure as part of their ongoing strike campaign to compel Saudi Arabia to halt military operations against the Houthis and accept the Houthis’ demands, which include lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-controlled ports and airports and granting the Houthis control over Yemen’s oil and gas resources.[40]

Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, October 23, 2026
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear. Ukrainian sources, including the Ukrainian General Staff and sources within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD), reported on October 23 that Ukrainian forces have observed “cases of connection loss” in Starlink/Starshield terminal operations at speeds of 161 kilometers per hour (around 100 miles per hour).[1] Sources within the Ukrainian MoD stated that there has been “no confirmation” about the removal of in-motion speed restrictions.[2] Ukrainian defense minister Serhii Sternenko stated that the situation with Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions “remains ambiguous” since some Ukrainian units report the resumption of operations at speeds exceeding the previously established limits, but the resumption does not apply to all missions, and he noted that some disruptions continue.[3] The situation regarding in-motion Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions remains unclear, but Ukrainian sources are emphasizing that Ukrainian forces continue experiencing problems with accessing Starlink/Starshield terminals as of October 23.
Russia and Ukraine have reportedly agreed to a limited ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast. The White House reported on October 23 that US First Lady Melania Trump secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Russia-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast beginning on October 29 to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation from the city amid a dire humanitarian crisis.[4] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on October 23 the White House’s press release and noted that Ukraine and Russia agreed to conduct a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, including securing a limited ceasefire, delivering humanitarian cargo to the city, and ensuring the free movement of civilians from the settlement.[5] Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov confirmed on October 23 that Russia agreed to the limited ceasefire in the Kherson direction beginning at 0400 local Moscow time on October 27 — a notably different start date from the one given in the White House press release.[6]
Russian occupation authorities are fully responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and have repeatedly and deliberately blocked evacuation and humanitarian routes into the settlement since the beginning of Russia's occupation.[7] Russian occupation authorities stopped the delivery of food and other critical supplies into Oleshky in late December 2025 and have failed to deliver any food or medicine to Oleshky since May 2026. The Kremlin rejected three local humanitarian ceasefire proposals from Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in May, July, and September 2026, after which Ukrainian forces conducted an operation to provide food to Oleshky residents via drone drops in September 2026.[8] Russian authorities have long refused to address the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and Gerasimov’s October 23 statement is the first instance of a Russian attempt to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”. Putin claimed on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is “the territory of historical Russia” while rejecting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline as part of a ceasefire agreement.[9] Putin also claimed that the “latest genetic research” identifies Russians and Ukrainians as “one people.” Putin’s October 22 reference to “historical Russia” likely refers to "Novorossiya" — an amorphous invented region in southern and eastern Ukraine that the Kremlin has claimed is “integral” to Russia.[10] Novorossiya notably includes not only Crimea and the four oblasts that Russia has illegally annexed (Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts), but also Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa oblasts.[11] Putin’s invocation of Russia’s historical claims demands that Ukraine surrender the Ukrainian-controlled 20.5 percent of Donetsk Oblast, 24.5 percent of Zaporizhia Oblast, including Zaporizhzhia City with a pre-war population of over 700,000 people, and 30 percent of Kherson Oblast, including Kherson City with a pre-war population of nearly 300,000 people. Putin’s October 23 statement explicitly demonstrates that Russian demands extend far beyond Ukraine’s Fortress Belt and Donetsk Oblast and may include the entire territory of Ukraine . Putin also emphasized his commitment to achieving all Russian war goals, which include the Russian demand for Ukraine’s full capitulation.[12] Putin’s statement demonstrates that the Kremlin is willing to participate in “negotiations” with Ukraine solely for the purpose of accepting Kyiv's surrender — not for the purpose of coming to some compromise peace agreement.
Putin also agreed to discuss the “European security architecture as a whole” after ensuring Ukraine’s and Russia’s future security.[13] Putin’s comment on “revising” the European security architecture refers to another Russian long-standing demand first articulated in the December 2021 ultimatum preceding the full-scale invasion that includes halting the deployment of military forces and weapons systems to NATO states that joined the alliance after 1997 and granting Russia a veto over certain NATO exercises.[14] Putin’s December 2021 demands are incompatible with US President Donald Trump’s commitment to maintaining a US military presence in Poland and the current US troop deployments in the Baltic States.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB). The Russian Central Bank announced on October 23 that it would keep the key interest rate at 14 percent for the second consecutive month, after lowering the rate 10 times over the past 18 months, citing elevated price pressure and high inflation expectations.[15] The Central Bank’s baseline scenario assumes an average key interest rate of 12.5 to 13.5 percent in 2027 — only 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points below the current rate. The Central Bank noted that underlying price growth is “not slowing” and identified pro-inflationary risks (or risk factors that increase inflation over the medium term), including price growth between five and six percent and estimated annual inflation of 6.8 percent. The Central Bank estimated that annual inflation will range between 7.1 and 7.6 percent by the end of 2026, a slight increase from the Central Bank’s September 11 announcement, and noted that volatile items like motor fuel (an oblique reference to the effects of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure) will continue impacting price dynamics. Russian Central Bank Chairwoman Elvira Nabiullina stated on October 23 that supply and demand continue facing inflationary risks, elevated inflation expectations, labor market tensions, and a larger budget deficit.[16] Nabiullina stated that Russia has experienced a decrease in consumer activity and that Russia’s GDP growth estimates for 2026 are between 0.5 and one percent. Nabiullina stated that the Central Bank is aiming to return the inflation rate to four percent in 2027.
The Russian Central Bank’s continued reduction of the key interest rate over an 18-month period prior to September 2026 likely contributed to domestic inflationary pressures.[17] Nabiullina has consistently expressed the need for monetary restraint — often trying to resist the Kremlin’s demands to expand capital availability for the Russian DIB and devalue the ruble to increase export revenues, despite ongoing fiscal inflationary pressures.[18] The Central Bank’s apparent success in avoiding further interest rate reductions at this time indicates that Putin has likely become more tolerant of contractionary monetary policy. Putin has recently prioritized reducing inflation to secure support amongst the Russian population by attempting to reduce the economic effects of Russian war spending, a prioritization that may have led him to accept Nabiullina’s fiscal policy for now.[19] Keeping the key rate at the current level will likely suppress wage growth and limit the amount of capital available to the Russian DIB, which may prevent Putin from achieving his goals of raising Russians’ effective purchasing power and maintaining the DIB’s production capacity. It remains difficult to assess, however, what effect fiscal policy will have on wage inflation and Russians’ quality of life, since Russia’s persistent labor shortages drive wage inflation for employed individuals while households face pressures that nominal wage figures do not capture.[20]
A likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship off the coast of Romania and drone debris fell in Moldova on October 23. Romanian President Nicusor Dan stated on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck a Comoros-flagged Khoryv cargo ship “near Romanian territorial waters” and added that the strike is a consequence of “Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.”[21] The Romanian Naval Authority reported that the Khoryv vessel sent a distress signal about 13 nautical miles (around 24 kilometers and just outside of the Romanian territorial waters) off the coast of Constanta, Romania.[22] European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the October 23 drone strike yet another “Russian escalation” in the Black Sea.[23] Territorial waters extend up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometers) from the country's shoreline, and states have sovereignty and jurisdiction over their territorial waters.[24] The October 23 drone strike comes against the backdrop of recent escalating Russian strikes against vessels in the Black Sea, including likely Russian drone strikes against two commercial tankers within Romanian territorial waters on October 14 and 15 and strikes against civilian vessels in the Bulgarian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) overnight on October 12 to 13.[25] The Moldovan police separately reported on October 23 that drone debris fell up to 100 meters from a residential building near Chistelnica, Telenesti Raion, Moldova.[26] These continuous, likely Russian violations of Moldovan and Romanian sovereign territory demonstrate Russia’s increasing willingness to pursue strike tactics that may directly impact the territory of NATO or NATO-aligned states.[27]
Ukraine and Russia conducted civilian prisoner and prisoner of war (POW) exchanges on October 23. Ukrainian and Russian authorities reported on October 23 that Ukraine and Russia exchanged 270 prisoners each.[28] Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported that Russia returned nine civilian prisoners back to Ukraine as part of the exchange.[29] Ukrainian Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of POWs reported that the October 23 POW exchange is the third stage of a combined prisoner swap that began on August 19, 2026.[30] Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets separately reported that Russia and Ukraine exchanged seven more civilians on October 23.[31]

We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.
Ukrainian forces launched a large strike package toward Moscow City, prompting the suspension of operations at all four Moscow area airports and the evacuation of government administrative buildings. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed on October 23 that 155 Ukrainian drones targeted Moscow Oblast overnight on October 22 and 23.[32] Russian state aviation regulator Rosaviatsia announced on October 23 that Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports — all four major airports servicing Moscow City — introduced temporary restrictions.[33] A Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) channel posted an image on October 23 showing drone debris on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo Airport.[34] The channel also published footage on October 23 purporting to show balloons flying over Moscow City, purportedly carrying explosives or small drones.[35] Russian opposition outlet Astra reported on October 23 that Russian authorities evacuated the IQ-Quarter tower in Moscow City, which reportedly houses offices for the Russian Ministries of Economic Development, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, the Ministry of Digital Development, and the Federal Agency for Technical Regulation and Metrology.[36]
Ukrainian forces conducted a series of long-range strikes against a Russian defense industrial facility, a chemical production plant, and administrative and military infrastructure in Russia. Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows the moment of a likely Ukrainian missile strike against the Proton plant in Oryol City, Oryol Oblast (roughly 161 kilometers from the frontline).[37] A Ukrainian OSINT channel stated that reportedly Ukrainian Storm Shadow cruise missiles struck the plant.[38] Ukrainian defense source Militarnyi reported that the plant manufactures components for the Russian S-71 Kover cruise missiles, Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.[39] Geolocated footage published on October 23 shows a Ukrainian FP-1 drone approaching the Azot UralKhim Chemical Plant in Berezniki, Perm Krai (roughly 1,585 kilometers from the international border) and smoke plumes rising from the facility.[40] Perm Krai governor Dmitry Makhonin acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian forces struck and damaged an industrial facility.[41] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted footage on October 23 purporting to show Ukrainian forces striking a Russian Federal Taxation Service data center in Gorodets, Nizhny Novgorod Oblast (roughly 785 kilometers from the international border).[42] Nizhny Novgorod Oblast Governor Gleb Nikitin acknowledged on October 23 that drone debris damaged unspecified infrastructure in Gorodets raion.[43] A Ukrainian OSINT channel posted on October 23 an image showing smoke plumes near Baltimore Air Base in Voronezh City (roughly 190 kilometers from the international border).[44] The channel reported that preliminary information indicates that Ukrainian forces targeted the former Voronezh Military Aviation Engineering University and an adjacent military aircraft parking area.[45] Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev acknowledged on October 23 that Ukrainian drones targeted Voronezh City.[46]
Russian objective: Create defensible buffer zones in Sumy Oblast along the international border
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations in northern Sumy Oblast on October 23 but did not advance.[47]
Russian objective: Push Ukrainian forces back from the international border to create a defensible buffer zone with Belgorod Oblast and approach Kharkiv City
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions northeast and northwest of Kharkiv City. Ukrainian forces struck Russian positions southeast of Khrypuny (northeast of Kharkiv City) and south of Nova Kozacha (northwest of Kharkiv City), according to geolocated footage published on October 20 and 22, respectively, after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[48]
Russian forces continued offensive operations northeast of Velykyi Burluk on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[49]
Russian objective: Cross the Oskil River in Kharkiv Oblast and push westward into eastern Kharkiv Oblast and northern Donetsk Oblas t
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Kupyansk direction on October 22 and 23 but did not make confirmed advances.[50]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Borova direction on October 23.
Russian Main Effort: Capture Ukraine's Fortress Belt and complete the seizure of Donetsk Oblast
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #1 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the northwest
Russian objective: Seize Lyman and cross the Siverskyi Donets River to support a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt – assessed objective of the Russian 25th Combined Arms Army and Western Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Lyman direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance.[51] A Russian milblogger claimed on October 23 that Russian forces are developing an offensive from Yampil (southeast of Lyman) towards Ozerne (southwest of Yampil) and Dibrova (west of Yampil).[52]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #2 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the east
Russian objective: Advance on Slovyansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkivka from the east – assessed objective of the Russian 3rd Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces continued limited offensive operations east of Slovyansk on October 23.[53] Donetsk Oblast Military Administration Head Vadym Filashkin ordered on October 22 the mandatory evacuation of all families with children in Kramatorsk and Slovyansk hromadas due to ongoing Russian strikes against civilian and residential infrastructure.[54]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #3 – Advance on the Fortress Belt from the south
Russian objective: Advance on Kostyantynivka and Druzhkivka from the south and southwest, east of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 8th Combined Arms Army and Southern Grouping of Forces elements
Ukrainian forces recently advanced west of Kostyantynivka. Ukrainian forces recently advanced in northern Sofiivka, according to geolocated footage published on October 22.[55]
Russian Subordinate Main Effort #4 – Encircle the Fortress Belt from the southwest
Russian objective: Conduct a wide encirclement of the Fortress Belt from near Dobropillya and Pokrovsk west of the Kazenyi Torets River – assessed objective of the Russian 51st Combined Arms Army and Central Grouping of Forces elements
Russian forces recently conducted an infiltration mission in southern Dobropillya. Russian forces are operating in southern Dobropillya, according to geolocated footage published on October 22, after what ISW assesses was a Russian infiltration mission.[56] Ukrainian military observer Kostyantyn Mashovets reported on October 21 that Russian forces infiltrated southern Dobropillya.[57]
Russian sources continue to use likely AI-generated or AI-altered footage to make aggrandized claims in the Dobropillya direction. A Russian source published footage on October 23 purportedly showing Russian forces raising flags in Vesele Pole (north of Dobropillya and roughly 12 kilometers from the furthest assessed extent of Russian advances).[58] ISW has reason to believe that the Russian flag raising video may be AI-generated or AI-altered, which would be consistent with previous Russian information operations that use AI footage to claim battlefield advances.[59]
Russian Supporting Effort: Advance into Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Russian objective: Interdict Ukrainian ground lines of communication that support Ukrainian positions in Donetsk Oblast and envelop Ukrainian positions in southwestern Donetsk Oblast – assessed objective of elements of the Russian Central and Eastern groupings of forces
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Novopavlivka and Oleksandrivka directions on October 23.
Russian objective: Maintain frontline positions, secure rear areas against Ukrainian strikes, and advance within tube artillery range of Zaporizhzhia City – assessed objective of the Russian Eastern and Dnepr Grouping of Forces
Russian forces continued offensive operations in the Hulyaipole direction on October 22 and 23 but did not advance as Ukrainian forces counterattacked in the area.[60]
Russian forces recently conducted infiltration missions west of Orikhiv. Ukrainian forces struck Russian positions in eastern Stepnohirsk, according to geolocated footage published on October 22, after what ISW assesses were Russian infiltration missions.[61] A Russian milblogger claimed on October 23 that Russian forces advanced south of Lukyanivske (west of Orikhiv).[62]
Ukrainian forces continued their intermediate-range strike campaign against Russian drone operators in occupied Zaporizhia Oblast. The Ukrainian General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Rubikon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies manpower concentration near Kamyanka, Zaporizhia Oblast (roughly 31 kilometers from the frontline) on October 22 or overnight on October 22 to 23.[63]
Neither Russian nor Ukrainian sources reported ground activity in the Kherson direction on October 23.

Embassies on alert as Iran ramps up threats, U.S. elections loom
U.S. embassy officials in the Middle East were on high alert as new reports said Iran is in "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans.
The alerts followed the U.S. order for non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week.
The Trump administration has vowed renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.
U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.
A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well.
The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group Saturday, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu.
Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June. Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal.
The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.
Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high . U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel.
